 Milan Momcilovic plays the most minutes but has the smallest offensive role, according to KenPom
 Drew Franklin @ DrewFranklinKSR 6h 0 Add as preferred source Add Share Add as preferred source Add Share 
 Milan Momcilovic needs to shoot more. Everyone knows that. Kentucky’s six-million-dollar man was brought to Lexington to be the Wildcats’ new sharpshooter, but five games into his first season with Mark Pope, he hasn’t been featured enough in the offense.
 Momcilovic and Kentucky failed their first big test together last week in the Champions Classic in Chicago. Momcilovic didn’t attempt a three in the first half against Kansas and finished the game with just five points on 1-for-3 shooting from outside. Even then, his one three-pointer was a contested fadeaway in the corner once the game was out of reach.
 Looking ahead to Kentucky’s second marquee game, Mark Pope told CBS Sports , “Milan is having such an impact on the game that’s not only shots… Clearly, everywhere he steps on the floor, he has so much gravity. And on top of that, if we could get him more shots and more shots and more shots, I’d like to do that also.”
 We’d all like for Pope to get Momcilovic more shots, starting tonight against Indiana. You go out and get Momcilovic to help you win games like this one. You pay him more than the Philadelphia Sixers are paying LeBron James this season to shoot the basketball. Yet, so far, Momcilovic hasn’t been the gunslinger that everyone envisioned. He’s making 40% of his three-pointers through five games, but his usage rate is criminally low.
 14.6% usage rate, according to KenPom
 Looking at KenPom ‘s breakdown of Kentucky’s contributors, Momcilovic falls into the “Limited Role” category for players who finish 12-16% of their team’s possessions while on the court. That’s beneath the “Role Players” (16-20%), “Significant Contributors” (20-24%), and “Major Contributors” (24-28%). 
 To be clear, usage rate measures the percentage of a team’s possessions that a player finishes with a shot, free throws, or a turnover. It doesn’t tell the whole story, but it shows how rarely Kentucky’s best weapon is finishing offensive possessions compared to his teammates.
 Malachi Moreno is the one major contributor, per KenPom:
 Malachi Moreno: Major Contributor (27.0%)
 Zoom Diallo: Significant Contributor (22.4%)
 Alex Wilkins: Significant Contributor (20.7%)
 Mason Williams: Significant Contributor (20.5%)
 Franck Kepnang: Significant Contributor (20.2%)
 Kam Williams: Significant Contributor (20.0%)
 Justin McBride: Role Player (17.0%)
 Braydon Hawthorne: Role Player (16.7%)
 Ousmane N’Diaye: Role Player (16.2%)
 Milan Momcilovic: Limited Role (14.6%) 
 Momcilovic is the only “Limited Role” guy, despite being one of the most talented and accomplished offensive players on the roster.
 Making things worse, Momcilovic leads Kentucky at 32.4 minutes per game . He’s paid more than anyone else and plays more than anyone else, yet KenPom classifies him as a limited-role player when it comes to offensive possessions used.
 More shots in the biggest games
 Despite the low usage rate, Momcilovic still averages seven three-point attempts a game. Pope has said he wants that number to be 10, but it’s not like Momcilovic isn’t shooting at all. It’s really the Kansas game that was so disappointing because it was the only time Kentucky has faced real competition so far this season, and he wasn’t a factor.
 Against Indiana, Kentucky should be more intentional about getting him looks. Get him involved with dribble handoffs and have him run off screens until his legs are ready to fall off. Even better, make Indiana chase him around until their legs fall off. If Pope wants more shots out of Momcilovic, it’s on him to help create them. We’ll see how that looks here soon in Indianapolis.
